title: Commercial Christmas Wreaths, Garland and Bows: A Sizing Guide
metaTitle: Commercial Christmas Wreath Sizing Guide for Buildings
metaDescription: Size commercial Christmas wreaths, garland and bows for doors, facades and parking structures in Canada: diameters, garland footage, bow sizes and mounting.
excerpt: Wreaths that look right at the door look tiny on a facade. This guide gives facility managers and BIA coordinators the sizing rules for commercial Christmas wreaths, garland and structural bows, plus pre-lit power, mounting hardware and wind planning.
heroAlt: Oversized commercial Christmas wreath with a large red structural bow mounted on a brick building facade in Ontario
keyTakeaways: Size wreaths to the architecture: roughly 3 ft over a door, 6 to 8 ft on a facade and 10 to 12 ft on a parking structure or tall blank wall.
Garland comes in 10 ft sections about 12 to 14 inches in diameter, so measure the linear feet of your railings and door frames and round up to whole sections.
A bow should be roughly half the diameter of the wreath it sits on, and structural bows from 15 to 60 inches are built to hold that shape in wind.
Pre-lit wreaths and garland are low power at roughly 10 W for a 3 ft wreath with 100 lights, so the real planning work is the outlet location, not circuit load.
Anchor every large wreath at four points with cable or stainless hardware, and order wind-rated frames for anything on an exposed elevation.

body.text: Wreaths, garland and bows are the lowest-power, lowest-labour way to dress a commercial building for Christmas, and they are also the easiest to get wrong. A wreath that looks generous on a retail door disappears on a three-storey facade. Garland ordered by guesswork leaves gaps at railing ends. A bow that is too small makes a big wreath look unfinished. This guide gives you the sizing rules we use for malls, BIAs, municipalities and property managers, along with the lighting, mounting and wind details that decide whether the install lasts the season.
Start with the building, not the product

Stand across the street, or in the parking lot, at the distance most people will see the building from. Anything you plan to hang has to read from there. A good test is to hold up a measured reference, such as a 3 ft cardboard circle, at the planned location and take a photo from the main approach. If you cannot see it clearly in the photo, go up a size.

Group the building into zones before you order: entrances and doors, windows and storefronts, railings and canopies, upper facade and roofline, and any structure such as a parking garage. Each zone gets its own size rule, which keeps the total order sensible and the finished look consistent.
Wreath diameter by location

Commercial [wreaths and garland](/product-category/garlands-and-wreathes) run from 3 ft up to 12 ft across. The sizing logic is simple: wreath diameter should be roughly one fifth to one third of the visible height or width of the surface it hangs on.

items: 3 ft: over a single door or at the centre of a window. This is the minimum size that reads from the sidewalk.
4 to 5 ft: double doors, wide storefront windows and lobby entrances. Use one per door leaf or one centred above the pair.
6 to 8 ft: building facades, one per structural bay between windows, spaced evenly. Use a 6 ft wreath on a two-storey face and 8 ft on three storeys.
10 to 12 ft: parking structures, tall blank walls, clock towers and mall entrance towers. Anything below 10 ft looks small at that scale.

body.text: For repeating wreaths along a facade, space them at about two diameters apart, centre to centre. A row of 6 ft wreaths on a 60 ft wall works best as five wreaths at 12 ft centres, which leaves even margins. Always use an odd count when there is a centre feature such as a door, so the pattern is symmetrical.
Quick rule: wreath diameter in feet is about the mounting height in feet divided by 3. A wreath hung 18 ft up should be about 6 ft across.
Garland: measure in linear feet

Commercial garland is sold in 10 ft sections, 12 to 14 inches in diameter, which is full enough to read from the street. Measure the length of every run in linear feet, add the drop at each end, and round up to the next full section. Garland can be joined end to end with the connecting wires, so there is no penalty for splitting a run across two sections.

items: Door frame, 7 ft high by 3 ft wide: 7 + 7 + 3 = 17 ft, so two sections (20 ft) with a bow at each top corner or one at the centre.

Railing run: measure the top rail, then add 1 ft per post if you plan to swag between posts rather than run straight. A 40 ft rail with swags every 8 ft needs about 50 ft of garland, which is five sections.
Storefront window frame, 8 ft by 5 ft: perimeter is 26 ft, so three sections.
Canopy or awning edge: use the full edge length, and order one extra section for the return at each end.

body.text: Garland attaches best at every 18 to 24 inches with zip ties or floral wire on a handrail, and every 12 inches on a vertical element. Use garland clips on aluminum railings so you do not scratch the finish. If you plan to light the garland, order lit sections now rather than adding strands later, since the lights are laid into the branch structure for a cleaner result.
Bows: roughly half the wreath

Bow size is a proportion problem. As a rule, the bow should be about half the diameter of the wreath it sits on, or slightly less on very large wreaths. [Commercial bows](/product-category/commercial-bows) run from 15 to 60 inches wide and are built on a structural base so they hold their shape in wind rather than flopping open after a week.

items: 10 to 12 ft wreath: 60 inch bow, which is the largest structural size and still proportionate.

body.text: Place the bow at the top (12 o’clock) for a classic look, or at the bottom for a more contemporary one. On garland, size bows at 15 to 24 inches and space them every 4 to 5 ft along a run. Match the bow material to the setting: weatherproof ribbon with a stiffened edge for exposed elevations, and velvet-look finishes only under cover.
Pre-lit wreaths and garland: the power picture

LED pre-lit wreaths draw very little power. As a planning figure, count roughly 0.1 W per light: a 3 ft wreath with about 100 lights is around 10 W, a 6 ft wreath with about 300 lights is around 30 W, and a 12 ft wreath with 600 lights is around 60 W. Confirm the exact wattage on each product page when you build your electrical plan.

That means one 15 A circuit, which gives you 1,440 W at the 80% continuous-load limit, can carry dozens of large wreaths. The limits you actually hit are practical ones: cord length, outlet location and voltage drop on long extension runs. Plan the power route when you plan the placement. Put outdoor receptacles within 25 to 50 ft of each wreath, and use outdoor-rated [extension cords and wire](/product-category/extension-cords-and-wire) with in-line connections wrapped or boxed so they stay dry.

Put each zone on a timer or photocell, and group wreaths that share a circuit. A mixed zone where lit wreaths and non-lit garland share a run is fine, but it is worth tagging the plug end of each so crews can swap a wreath quickly if a section fails.
Mounting hardware and wind

Wreaths act like sails. A 10 ft wreath presents roughly 80 square feet of surface, and in a 70 km/h gust the load on the anchor points can be considerable. Plan mounting around the hardest wind you realistically expect, not the average day.

items: Use four attachment points on any wreath over 5 ft: top, bottom and both sides. A single hook at the top will let the wreath swing and chafe.
Use stainless steel cable, rated turnbuckles and corrosion-resistant fasteners. Galvanized carbon steel stains masonry as it rusts.
On masonry, use sleeve or wedge anchors sized by the installer. On metal cladding, use through-bolts with backing plates.
On parking structures and parapets, use rooftop brackets or a clamp system. Have the building owner or an engineer approve any attachment to the structure.
For exposed elevations, choose open-frame or wind-rated wreaths and add a tensioned cable at the bottom to stop flutter.

body.text: Check the install halfway through the season, and after each major storm. Look for loose ties, chafed cords and bows that have shifted. For commercial properties with many installs, a short inspection checklist saves both repair time and liability risk.
Putting an order together

List each zone, its size rule and its quantity. Round garland up to whole 10 ft sections, choose bow sizes at half the wreath diameter, and add a spare bow and a spare garland section per 10 of each, since transit and install wear happen. Pair wreaths and garland with the matching [pole-mount décor](/product-category/pole-mount-decor) if the property also has light poles to dress.

Add everything to your cart and submit an inquiry. The team replies by email, usually within one business day, with shipping cost, timeline and any volume pricing. Free shipping applies on orders over $150, and municipalities and BIAs can request net-30 invoicing, tax-exempt handling and RFP-ready line-item quotes. Professional installers can ask about the [installer program](/professional-installer).
Order by late September for a mid-November install. Large wreaths and structural bows are the first items to run short in October.

faq.q: What size wreath should go over a commercial door?
faq.a: A 3 ft wreath is the minimum that reads from the sidewalk over a single door. For double doors or a wide lobby entrance, move up to 4 or 5 ft so the wreath keeps its proportion to the opening.

faq.q: How much garland do I need for a railing?
faq.a: Measure the railing in linear feet and round up to the next 10 ft section. If you plan to swag between posts, add about 1 ft per post. For example, a 40 ft rail swagged every 8 ft needs about 50 ft, or five sections.

faq.q: How big should the bow be on a large wreath?
faq.a: Roughly half the diameter of the wreath. A 6 ft wreath takes a 30 to 36 inch bow, and a 10 to 12 ft wreath takes a 60 inch structural bow, which is the largest size available.

faq.q: How much power do pre-lit wreaths use?
faq.a: Very little. As a planning figure, a 3 ft LED wreath with about 100 lights draws around 10 W, so one 15 A circuit can carry many wreaths. Confirm the exact wattage on each product page.

faq.q: Can large wreaths handle Canadian winter wind?
faq.a: Yes, if they are mounted at four points with cable or stainless hardware and you choose open-frame or wind-rated wreaths for exposed elevations. Check the mounting after every major storm.
